title: Language Models and Generation
summary: This intermediate-level module explains how a language model generates text from next-token probabilities. After completing it, a learner can distinguish probability estimation from decoding, compare common decoding approaches, and identify why generated claims still require verification.
objectives: Explain how repeated next-token prediction produces a sequence.
Distinguish a model's probability distribution from the decoding procedure that selects a token.
Compare greedy selection, unrestricted sampling, and nucleus sampling.
Explain why a probable continuation is not necessarily a factually correct continuation.

sections.title: Level and foundations
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It requires no prerequisite module, but it uses basic probability language. A probability distribution assigns each possible outcome a number from zero to one, with the probabilities across all considered outcomes summing to one.

A token is a unit in the sequence processed by a language model. Given preceding tokens as context, an autoregressive language model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens. Generation repeats a cycle: calculate the next-token distribution, select a token, append it to the context, and continue until a stopping condition is reached.

sections.title: Separate the model from decoding
paragraphs: The model produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens. A decoding procedure uses that distribution to choose what comes next. This distinction matters because the same distribution can lead to different continuations when different decoding procedures are used.

Greedy selection chooses the highest-probability token at every step. It is deterministic when there is a unique highest-probability token, but repeatedly taking the local maximum does not guarantee the best complete passage.

Unrestricted sampling randomly selects among possible tokens according to their probabilities. Nucleus sampling first restricts selection to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a chosen threshold, then samples from that set. Research on neural text generation introduced nucleus sampling as an alternative to likelihood-maximizing decoding and fixed candidate-set sampling.

sections.title: Probability is not a truth test
paragraphs: A next-token probability represents the model's relative preference among possible continuations in the current context. It does not independently establish that a continuation is true.

A fluent sentence can therefore contain an unsupported or incorrect claim. When factual accuracy matters, evaluate the claim using appropriate external evidence rather than treating fluency or model probability as verification.
sections.callout: Keep two questions separate: What continuation does the model favor, and what evidence shows that the continuation is true?

sections.title: Analyze a generation process
paragraphs: To analyze generated text, first identify the context supplied to the model. Next, distinguish the probability-producing model from the procedure used to select each token. Then consider how that selection procedure can affect repetition, variety, and predictability. Finally, verify factual claims separately.
This sequence of analysis prevents a common category error: attributing every property of an output to the model alone when the decoding procedure also helped determine which continuation appeared.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes autoregressive text generation?
choices: Select an entire passage first, then assign probabilities to its tokens.
Calculate a next-token distribution, select a token, append it to the context, and repeat.
Verify every possible sentence, then return the shortest verified sentence.
Choose tokens without using the preceding context.
questions.explanation: The module describes generation as a repeated cycle of calculating next-token probabilities, selecting one token, appending it, and continuing.

questions.prompt: What does greedy selection choose at each generation step?
choices: The token with the highest probability at that step.
A random token from the entire token set.
The complete passage with the greatest verified accuracy.
questions.explanation: Greedy selection chooses the highest-probability next token at every step.

questions.prompt: What does a high next-token probability establish?
choices: That the resulting factual claim has been independently verified.
That the token is relatively favored by the model in the current context.
That every decoding procedure must select the token.
That the complete passage is the best possible passage.
questions.explanation: A next-token probability represents the model's relative preference in context. It is not independent evidence that a generated claim is true.
